items.item: The same graph model (entities as nodes, relationships as named edges) is what makes a catalog's search, trust and glossary features possible at all — each is a different traversal or filter over the same underlying graph, not three separate systems.

items.item: A crawl's staleness window is a direct function of its schedule, never of how good the crawler is — a smarter crawler run on the same weekly schedule still leaves the same week-long gap.

items.item: Technical catalog versus business catalog is a distinction in audience and question, not in product: a single tool like Unity Catalog or DataHub typically answers both kinds of question for different users, rather than the two being separate product categories.

items.item: The tags a catalog's glossary and business metadata carry on a column are the same classification output topic 4 produces — this topic is where that classification becomes something searchable and attached to an owner, not a new classification step.

The predict question's two scenarios (crawl-faster vs push, then tables-pushed-but-dashboards-crawled) both test the same underlying claim from different angles: staleness is a property of an integration's own update mechanism, not a single dial the whole catalog shares.

items.item: Apache Polaris and Unity Catalog's open edition are both named as technical catalogs specifically because they sit on top of an open table format (Chapter 6's own subject) rather than wrapping a proprietary storage layer, which is what lets either one serve as a shared catalog across engines.
